issues.legal_issue: The business need that permits eviction from nonresidential accommodation means a need for the landlord’s own occupation of the premises to conduct business.
material_facts: The landlord sought possession of nonresidential premises to continue a partnership business in which he was one of three partners, the other partners being his brothers.
The lower courts treated the partnership business as the landlord’s business without examining the statutory setting of the phrase.
issues.conclusion: A landlord’s business need under Section 12(1)(f) requires that the premises be needed for the landlord’s own occupation by way of conducting business; being a partner alone does not establish that the partnership’s business is the landlord’s business for this purpose.
issues.legal_principle: The phrase must be construed in light of the Act’s purpose of fairly distributing scarce accommodation and the setting of Section 12(1)(f). Sections 12(1)(e) and (f), 12(4)–(6), 17, 18 and 39(2) show that the Act protects tenants of nonresidential accommodation more strictly and connect the business ground for eviction to the landlord’s own occupation. The Court distinguished Rajniklal and Co. v. Vithal Pandurang Kawade because it construed different wording without considering the statutory setting; it also explained that the income-tax cases Commissioner of Income-tax, West Bengal v. A. W. Figgies and Co. and Dulichand Lakshminarayan v. Commissioner of Income-tax concerned materially different statutory provisions. Tansukhdas Chhaganlal, Karsandas Ramji and Gundalapalli Rangamannar Chetty concerned subletting and occupation, rather than the meaning of the statutory business-need ground.

predicates.landlord_business_eviction_case: A landlord sought to evict a tenant from nonresidential accommodation on a claimed need to use the premises for business.
predicates.landlord_claimed_business_use: The landlord said the premises were needed to conduct or continue a business.

issues.definition: When a landlord seeks eviction from nonresidential accommodation for business use, the claimed business need means a need for the landlord’s own occupation of the premises to conduct business.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord seeking nonresidential premises for a partnership business must prove that the premises are needed directly and substantially for the landlord’s own business occupation.
material_facts: The landlord said he and his brothers carried on a partnership business and sought the premises for that business.
The partnership registration certificate identified the partners, but the partnership deed was not produced.

The landlord did not establish that he was entitled to manage the business or that he would occupy the premises with the other partners; the evidence did not establish that the premises were needed directly and substantially for his own business occupation.
issues.conclusion: The landlord failed to prove the required personal business occupation, so the eviction suit had to be dismissed. The appeal was allowed and the lower courts’ decisions were set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 12(1)(f), read as requiring the landlord’s own occupation by way of continuing or starting business, the landlord must prove that the accommodation is needed directly and substantially for that occupation. Proof that the landlord is a partner, including a certificate showing the partners, does not by itself establish the required need. The Court’s discussion of Clift v. Taylor was consistent with the need for evidence that the landlord was a managing partner and would occupy the premises; Tunstall v. Steigamann concerned a business carried on by a separate incorporated company and did not assist in construing this provision.

predicates.landlord_business_eviction_case: A landlord sought to evict a tenant from nonresidential accommodation on a claimed need to use the premises for business.
predicates.partnership_business_was_proposed: The landlord proposed to use the premises for a business carried on in partnership with others.
predicates.personal_business_occupation_not_proved: The landlord did not prove that the premises were needed directly and substantially for the landlord’s own occupation to conduct the business.

issues.definition: If a landlord seeks nonresidential premises for a partnership business but does not prove the landlord’s own direct and substantial business occupation, the eviction claim fails.
